presentingComplaint: Cough for 6 days, initially dry now with some clear-to-yellow sputum, following a head cold
history: Previously well non-smoker presents with a 6-day history of cough. It began 2 days after coryzal symptoms (sore throat, nasal congestion, low-grade malaise). The cough was dry at first and is now occasionally productive of scanty mucoid, sometimes yellowish, sputum. He reports mild substernal discomfort with bouts of coughing but no pleuritic pain and no true breathlessness at rest. No haemoptysis, no night sweats, no weight loss. Several colleagues at work have had a similar 'chest cold'. No underlying lung disease, no asthma, no immunosuppression, no recent travel, no TB contact. Not on any regular medication; no drug allergies.
examination: Comfortable at rest, not toxic, well perfused. Mild pharyngeal erythema. Chest: normal expansion, resonant percussion, vesicular breath sounds with occasional scattered wheeze that clears on coughing; no focal crepitations, no bronchial breathing, no signs of consolidation. No lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular and abdominal examination unremarkable. Pertinent negatives: no localised crackles, no dullness, no accessory muscle use, no cyanosis.
imaging: Chest X-ray (obtained to exclude pneumonia given persistent cough): no consolidation, no effusion, normal cardiac silhouette and lung fields
microbiology: Not routinely indicated; if sent, sputum is scant and non-diagnostic. Most cases viral (rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza)
citations: Harrison 22e — Acute Bronchitis and Acute Tracheobronchitis
ACCP/CHEST Cough Due to Acute Bronchitis 2006
stewardship: No empiric antibiotic. Acute bronchitis in a previously healthy adult is overwhelmingly viral and self-limiting; normal vitals, absence of focal chest signs, normal CXR and low procalcitonin argue strongly against bacterial pneumonia. Manage symptomatically (fluids, antitussive/analgesia as needed); antibiotics do not shorten illness and drive resistance/adverse effects. Antibiotic stewardship: avoid antibiotics unless features of pneumonia, pertussis (targeted macrolide), or superimposed bacterial infection emerge.
contraindications: Avoid unnecessary macrolides/fluoroquinolones — QT prolongation and C. difficile risk without benefit
If pertussis suspected in pregnancy, azithromycin preferred over doxycycline
edgeCases: Cough can persist 2-3 weeks (post-bronchitic bronchial hyperreactivity) and does NOT imply treatment failure or need for antibiotics
Purulent (yellow/green) sputum reflects sloughed tracheobronchial epithelium and does NOT indicate bacterial infection
Whooping/paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting should prompt consideration of pertussis; focal crackles or hypoxia should prompt re-evaluation for pneumonia
expectedMaiK: This is a classic self-limiting acute bronchitis in a healthy adult; the constellation of normal vitals, absent focal chest findings, clear CXR and low procalcitonin makes bacterial pneumonia very unlikely, so antibiotics are not indicated. Advise symptomatic care and safety-net for hypoxia, high fever, or focal signs.
expectedNextQuestions: Any paroxysmal/whooping cough or post-tussive vomiting to suggest pertussis?
Any breathlessness at rest, high fever, rigors or pleuritic pain suggesting pneumonia?
Any history of asthma, smoking or prior similar episodes?
expectedInvestigations: No routine investigation needed in a well patient; chest X-ray only if pneumonia suspected (focal signs, high fever, tachypnoea, hypoxia, HR >100, or elderly)
Consider pertussis testing if paroxysmal cough >2 weeks

investigations: Chest X-ray only if pneumonia suspected
